nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; criticism, the Renaissance history and the literature of desire
literary_identity: Critic, historian of the Renaissance and poet; the author of Renaissance in Italy and one of the founders of the modern literature of male same-sex desire.
biography: Born at Bristol on 5 October 1840, the son of a physician; he was educated at Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford, where he fell in love with a Bristol chorister and wrote the sonnets that became part of his life's secret work. He married Janet North in 1864 and lived at Clifton and Davos, Switzerland, for his health. He wrote Renaissance in Italy (1875-86), biographies of Michelangelo and Ben Jonson, translations of Greek poetry and a large body of verse and prose on Greek love. He died at Rome on 19 April 1893.
literary_profile: Symonds wrote the history of the Renaissance as a history of feeling: his seven-volume Renaissance in Italy is the first full English account of the period as a whole, and his studies of Greek ethics, Walt Whitman and Michelangelo were the foundation of the modern study of same-sex desire in literature. He was a poet of considerable power and a prose writer of great range, and his private writings — the Memoirs and the 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' — are among the first sustained English arguments for the dignity of homosexual love.
stylistic_characteristics: Historical narrative on a large scale; biography as psychological analysis; the sonnet and the elegy; scholarly prose with a personal urgency; the translation as an act of identification; private manuscript and careful publication.
intellectual_concerns: The Renaissance and its culture of the individual; Greek ethics and the love of men; the relation of art to sexuality; Whitman and democratic comradeship; Italy and the Alps as scenes of self-discovery; the ethics of concealment.
historical_significance: Symonds wrote the first comprehensive English history of the Italian Renaissance and was the most important English writer on same-sex desire before Wilde's trials: his 'A Problem in Greek Ethics' (privately printed, 1883) is a founding text of the modern discourse, and his influence on Pater, Gosse, Havelock Ellis and the 1890s is decisive.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; criticism, biography and the history of ideas
literary_identity: Critic, biographer and mountaineer; the first editor of the Dictionary of National Biography and the greatest Victorian critic of the eighteenth century.
biography: Born in London on 28 November 1832, the son of the Under-Secretary of the Colonial Office; he was educated at Eton and Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and in 1862 was ordained. He lost his faith and left the church in 1875, and supported himself by journalism and scholarship: he was editor of the Cornhill Magazine (1871-82) and of the Dictionary of National Biography (1882-91), for which he wrote 378 lives. He married Harriet Marion Thackeray in 1867 and, after her death, Julia Jackson Duckworth in 1878, becoming the father of Vanessa Bell and Virginia Woolf. He died in Kensington on 22 February 1904.
literary_profile: Stephen is the great Victorian critic of the English eighteenth century and the founder of the modern biographical dictionary. His History of English Thought in the Eighteenth Century (1876) is a systematic account of the deist controversy and the moral philosophy of the age; his Hours in a Library, The English Utilitarians and the essays on Pope, Johnson and Swift are the foundation of the scholarly criticism of Augustan literature, and his agnostic 'Essays on Freethinking and Plainspeaking' made him the most formidable of Victorian rationalists.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, exact critical prose; the biographical reconstruction of a writer's mind; the systematic history of ideas; the mountaineering essay; the short life in the Dictionary; irony without malice.
intellectual_concerns: The history of ideas and the growth of rationalism; eighteenth-century literature and society; agnosticism and the ethics of unbelief; biography as a form of criticism; the Alps and the physical life; the education of women.
historical_significance: Stephen founded the Dictionary of National Biography and wrote the founding modern study of English eighteenth-century thought: he is the ancestor of the scholarly biography and of the history of ideas in England, and his agnostic essays are the classic statement of Victorian unbelief as a moral position.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; literary history, biography and the memoir
literary_identity: Poet, critic and biographer; the author of Father and Son, one of the greatest Victorian autobiographies, and the first English historian of modern literature.
biography: Born in London on 21 September 1849, the son of Philip Henry Gosse, the naturalist and Plymouth Brother; he was brought up in a strict Evangelical household and left it in 1867, an experience recorded in Father and Son (1907). He worked in the Department of Printed Books at the British Museum, became a prolific reviewer and translator, and was Clark Lecturer at Cambridge (1889-1901) and librarian of the House of Lords (1904-14). He did more than any other critic to introduce Ibsen and the Scandinavians to England, and he was knighted in 1925, dying in London on 16 May 1928.
literary_profile: Gosse's Father and Son is the classic Victorian memoir of a religious upbringing: it is a study of a father's faith and a son's escape, written with a novelist's sense of scene and a scientist's precision. His critical writing — A History of Eighteenth Century Literature, the lives of Donne, Congreve, Ibsen and Swinburne — made him the great Victorianiser and publicist of the modern, and he was the first English critic to take Ibsen seriously.
stylistic_characteristics: The scene-based memoir; ironic comedy of two incompatible minds; exact period detail; the critical survey with a clear narrative line; the biographical essay; translation from the Scandinavian and the French.
intellectual_concerns: Religious upbringing and the loss of faith; the conflict of generations; the history of English literature as a national narrative; the introduction of modern drama; biography as literary gossip and as scholarship; the Victorian literary world and its networks.
historical_significance: Gosse's Father and Son is one of the founding texts of the modern autobiography and the finest account we have of Victorian Evangelical family life; his critical histories and his promotion of Ibsen made him a central agent in the making of the modern English literary canon.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; criticism, folklore and the literary anthology
literary_identity: Poet, critic, folklorist and translator; the most versatile and prolific man of letters of the late Victorian period.
biography: Born at Selkirk on 31 March 1844; educated at Selkirk, Edinburgh Academy, St Andrews and Balliol College, Oxford, where he became a fellow. He settled in London in 1875 and supported himself entirely by journalism: he wrote leaders for the Daily News, reviews for the Fortnightly and the Contemporary, was editor of Longman's Magazine (1882-1905), and produced more than a hundred books. He is remembered for the twelve volumes of fairy tales (The Blue Fairy Book and its successors, 1889-1910) and for his work on Homer, ballads and folklore. He died at Banchory, Aberdeenshire, on 20 July 1912.
literary_profile: Lang was the great populariser of the Victorian literary world: he reviewed everything, edited everything, translated Homer into prose and Theocritus into verse, and argued successfully for the anthropological reading of fairy tales and mythology. His fairy books — with the illustrations of H. J. Ford and Lancelot Speed — were the most important single agency in making the world's folklore available to English children and shaped the twentieth-century fairy-tale canon.
stylistic_characteristics: Easy, witty, allusive journalism; the plain prose translation of Homer; metrical experiment in ballad and pastoral; the anthology as a literary form; the fairy tale retold with scholarly care.
intellectual_concerns: Folklore and the comparative study of myth; Homer and the epic; the Scottish ballads and Border tradition; the fairy tale as a common inheritance of mankind; romance and the literature of escape; the craft of reviewing.
historical_significance: Lang's fairy books created the modern canon of the fairy tale in English and made the world's folklore a children's inheritance; his Homer and his ballad scholarship were serious contributions, and his essays are the best record we have of the working literary journalism of the age.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the lyric, the essay and Catholic poetry
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; one of the finest religious lyric poets of the later nineteenth century and a central figure of the Catholic literary revival.
biography: Born Alice Christiana Gertrude Thompson in London on 22 September 1847, the daughter of a businessman and amateur artist; she was brought up partly in Italy and at fourteen was converted to Roman Catholicism. She married Wilfrid Meynell in 1877 and the couple edited the Catholic weekly Merry England (1883-95), publishing Francis Thompson, Lionel Johnson and the young Hilaire Belloc; she wrote essays for the Saturday Review, the Pall Mall Gazette and the Dublin Review. Two of her children died in infancy, and her later verse is marked by grief. She died in London on 27 November 1922.
literary_profile: Meynell wrote the lyric of concentrated stillness: her poems are short, exact, almost epigrammatic, and her prose essays are among the most beautiful in the language, moving from a leaf or a window to a considered thought about time, faith and the poor. She was a feminist by implication rather than by campaign, and her essay 'The Rhythm of Life' and her poem 'The Shepherdess' opened a space in English poetry for a woman's religious and maternal experience that was neither sentimental nor didactic.
stylistic_characteristics: Short lyric metres with a delicate rhythmic suspense; the single image held and turned; the essay as meditation; a Catholic sacramental vision of ordinary things; the withheld emotion and the plain word.
intellectual_concerns: Time, memory and mortality; Catholic faith and the sacramental world; the poverty of the London poor; the position of women and the woman artist; infancy and bereavement; the beauty of the ordinary.
historical_significance: Meynell is one of the finest English religious poets of the century: her poems are anthologised in every serious collection of Victorian verse, her essays are a permanent part of the English essay tradition, and as an editor she made Merry England the nursery of the Catholic literary revival that would produce Chesterton and Belloc.
major_influences: Alice Meynell's Catholic devotional reading (Thomas a Kempis, Francis de Sales)

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the New Woman lyric, the novel and Anglo-Jewish poetry
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and essayist; the first Jewish woman writer in English to make her own experience the centre of her art, and a central figure of the 1880s New Woman generation.
biography: Born in London on 10 November 1861 into an Anglo-Jewish family; she was the second Jewish woman to study at Cambridge, entering Newnham College in 1879, and was the first Jewish woman to graduate from the University of London, in 1884. She published three volumes of verse and two novels, wrote essays on Jewish life and on women's education, and was a friend of Clementina Black, Eleanor Marx and Olive Schreiner. She took her own life in her parents' house in London on 10 September 1889, at the age of twenty-seven.
literary_profile: Levy wrote the poetry of the modern woman in the modern city: her verse is formal, ironic, and alive with the noise of London, the reading room of the British Museum, the theatre and the omnibus; her novel Reuben Sachs (1888) is the first sustained English fiction of Anglo-Jewish middle-class life, and its satire of the community was denounced as a betrayal. She is the poet of a double minority, and her work is now central to the study of Victorian Jewish literature.
stylistic_characteristics: Metrical accomplishment in traditional forms (sonnet, ballad, dramatic monologue); urban imagery; ironic self-portraiture; a dry wit about courtship and the marriage market; the juxtaposition of Jewish and English worlds.
intellectual_concerns: The position of the educated woman; Anglo-Jewish identity and the pressure of community; London as a city of strangers; unrequited love and the refusal of marriage; the woman writer's ambition and its costs.
historical_significance: Levy is the founding figure of Anglo-Jewish women's writing in English and one of the most gifted poets of her generation: Reuben Sachs is a landmark of Victorian Jewish fiction, her essays on Jewish women and on the woman's vote are early feminist documents, and her poetry — recovered in the 1990s — has become central to the study of the 1880s.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: German-born English; the long poem, the lyric and women's biography
literary_identity: Poet, biographer and translator; a leading woman of letters of the 1870s-90s and the first English biographer of George Eliot.
biography: Born Mathilde Cohen in Mannheim on 21 March 1841; her mother remarried the revolutionary Karl Blind and the family settled in London in 1852 as political exiles. She was educated at a private school in London and became a freethinker, a feminist and an admirer of Mazzini and Shelley. She published The Prophecy of Saint Oran (1881), The Ascent of Man (1889) — a long evolutionary epic in blank verse — and a biography of George Eliot (1883), the first full life of the novelist. She died in London on 26 November 1896.
literary_profile: Blind wrote the poetry of evolution and of women's intellectual ambition: The Ascent of Man is a Victorian epic of Darwinian progress, and her lyrics and sonnets are among the most technically accomplished by a woman poet of the period. She was also a substantial critic and translator, and her life of George Eliot remains one of the most perceptive early accounts of the novelist.
stylistic_characteristics: Blank-verse narrative epic; the sonnet and the lyric; scientific and evolutionary imagery; rhetorical and oratorical periods; translation from the German and the French; the biography as critical study.
intellectual_concerns: Evolution and the ascent of humanity; freedom and political exile; women's intellectual life and the right to love freely; Greek myth and the tragic; death and the natural world; the European revolutionary tradition.
historical_significance: Blind was one of the most ambitious women poets of the century: her Darwinian epic is unique in Victorian verse, her biography of George Eliot is a founding work of the feminist criticism of the novel, and her translations and essays made German and French literature available to English readers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the dramatic poem, the sonnet and the woman's monologue
literary_identity: Poet, playwright, essayist and translator; the author of the finest Victorian dramatic monologues by a woman, and a campaigner for women's education and the vote.
biography: Born Julia Augusta Davies at Poole on 30 January 1837, the daughter of a naval officer; she was educated at the Cambridge home of her grandfather and at the South Kensington art school, and married the solicitor and philologist Thomas Webster in 1863. She published four volumes of poetry, the verse dramas Theaus (1867) and Medea (1878), a translation of Euripides, and three novels, and she campaigned for women's suffrage and against the Contagious Diseases Acts. She died at Kensington on 5 September 1894.
literary_profile: Webster wrote the dramatic monologue as a woman's form: 'A Castaway' is the greatest Victorian poem spoken by a prostitute, and 'Circe', 'The Happiest Girl in the World' and the Medea translation adapt the classical and the contemporary to a woman's voice. She was a learned and technically ambitious poet — her verse is dense, allusive and often deliberately difficult — and her essays on poetry and on women are among the sharpest of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The dramatic monologue with a fully realised speaker; classical and mythological subjects turned to modern use; dense, allusive, syntactically suspended verse; sonnet sequences; translation as interpretation.
intellectual_concerns: The position of women and the sexual double standard; the fallen woman and the prostitute's voice; marriage and the loss of self; classical myth as a vehicle for modern feeling; education and women's intellectual capacity; motherhood.
historical_significance: Webster is the most important woman writer of the Victorian dramatic monologue: 'A Castaway' is the classic Victorian poem on prostitution from the woman's own side, and her Medea is a landmark of nineteenth-century classical translation. Her work is now central to the recovery of Victorian women's poetry.
